claim: HDAC7 controls the thymic effector programming of Natural Killer T (NKT) cells.
source: We report that Histone Deacetylase 7 (HDAC7) controls the thymic effector programming of Natural Killer T (NKT) cells, and that interference with this function contributes to tissue-specific autoimmunity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: Interference with HDAC7 function contributes to tissue-specific autoimmunity.
source: We report that Histone Deacetylase 7 (HDAC7) controls the thymic effector programming of Natural Killer T (NKT) cells, and that interference with this function contributes to tissue-specific autoimmunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing autoimmune disease in HDAC7 gain-of-function mice and amelioration upon iNKT cell reconstitution.

claim: Gain of HDAC7 function in thymocytes blocks negative selection.
source: Gain of HDAC7 function in thymocytes blocks both negative selection and NKT development, and diverts Vα14/Jα18 TCR transgenic thymocytes into a Tconv-like lineage.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Kasler et al., 2012) and data in the current manuscript.

claim: Gain of HDAC7 function in thymocytes blocks NKT development.
source: Gain of HDAC7 function in thymocytes blocks both negative selection and NKT development, and diverts Vα14/Jα18 TCR transgenic thymocytes into a Tconv-like lineage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data showing near-complete absence of iNKT cells in HDAC7-ΔP mice (Figure 1A,B).

claim: Gain of HDAC7 function diverts Vα14/Jα18 TCR transgenic thymocytes into a Tconv-like lineage.
source: Gain of HDAC7 function in thymocytes blocks both negative selection and NKT development, and diverts Vα14/Jα18 TCR transgenic thymocytes into a Tconv-like lineage.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that Vα14 x HDAC7-ΔP iNKT cells exhibit naïve-like characteristics (Figure 3B-F).

claim: HDAC7 deletion promotes thymocyte apoptosis.
source: Conversely, HDAC7 deletion promotes thymocyte apoptosis and causes expansion of innate-effector cells.
evidence: This is supported by previous work (Kasler et al., 2011) showing increased apoptosis of DP thymocytes in Hdac7-KO mice.

claim: HDAC7 deletion causes expansion of innate-effector cells.
source: Conversely, HDAC7 deletion promotes thymocyte apoptosis and causes expansion of innate-effector cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data showing expansion of CD44hi Eomes+ cells in Hdac7-KO mice (Figure 2B).

claim: HDAC7 binds PLZF.
source: Investigating the mechanisms involved, we found that HDAC7 binds PLZF and modulates PLZF-dependent transcription.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 7A-E).

claim: HDAC7 modulates PLZF-dependent transcription.
source: Investigating the mechanisms involved, we found that HDAC7 binds PLZF and modulates PLZF-dependent transcription.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assays (Figure 7F) and RNA-seq data showing overlap between HDAC7 and PLZF targets (Figure 5B-C).

claim: HDAC7 is a human risk locus for IBD.
source: Moreover, HDAC7 and many of its transcriptional targets are human risk loci for IBD and PSC, autoimmune diseases that strikingly resemble the disease we observe in HDAC7 gain-of-function in mice.
evidence: This is based on GWAS studies cited (Liu et al., 2013; Jostins et al., 2012).

claim: HDAC7 is a human risk locus for PSC.
source: Moreover, HDAC7 and many of its transcriptional targets are human risk loci for IBD and PSC, autoimmune diseases that strikingly resemble the disease we observe in HDAC7 gain-of-function in mice.
evidence: This is based on GWAS studies cited (Liu et al., 2013; Jostins et al., 2012).

claim: Many HDAC7 transcriptional targets are human risk loci for IBD and PSC.
source: Moreover, HDAC7 and many of its transcriptional targets are human risk loci for IBD and PSC, autoimmune diseases that strikingly resemble the disease we observe in HDAC7 gain-of-function in mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis showing 81 of 176 GWAS risk loci are regulated by HDAC7 (Figure 6A).

claim: IBD and PSC strikingly resemble the disease observed in HDAC7 gain-of-function mice.
source: Moreover, HDAC7 and many of its transcriptional targets are human risk loci for IBD and PSC, autoimmune diseases that strikingly resemble the disease we observe in HDAC7 gain-of-function in mice.
evidence: This is based on comparison of tissue distribution of disease in HDAC7-ΔP mice with human IBD/PSC pathology.

claim: Reconstitution of iNKT cells in HDAC7 gain-of-function mice mitigated their disease.
source: Importantly, reconstitution of iNKT cells in these mice mitigated their disease, suggesting that the combined defects in negative selection and iNKT cells due to altered HDAC7 function can cause tissue-restricted autoimmunity, a finding that may explain the association between HDAC7 and hepatobiliary autoimmunity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data showing improved survival and reduced liver damage in Vα14:HDAC7-ΔP chimeras (Figure 8C-D).

claim: Combined defects in negative selection and iNKT cells due to altered HDAC7 function can cause tissue-restricted autoimmunity.
source: Importantly, reconstitution of iNKT cells in these mice mitigated their disease, suggesting that the combined defects in negative selection and iNKT cells due to altered HDAC7 function can cause tissue-restricted autoimmunity, a finding that may explain the association between HDAC7 and hepatobiliary autoimmunity.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing partial amelioration of disease upon iNKT reconstitution.

claim: iNKT cells represent approximately 3% of TCRβ-positive cells in wild type C57BL/6 thymus.
source: Cells positive for staining with CD1D/αGalCer tetramers represent approximately 3% of TCRβ-positive cells in wild type C57BL/6 (B6) thymus and 30% in liver, however they are nearly undetectable in either of these tissues or in the spleens or livers of HDAC7-ΔP mice (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, for full gating see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a profound deficiency in iNKT development.
evidence: This is quantified from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: iNKT cells represent approximately 30% of TCRβ-positive cells in wild type C57BL/6 liver.
source: Cells positive for staining with CD1D/αGalCer tetramers represent approximately 3% of TCRβ-positive cells in wild type C57BL/6 (B6) thymus and 30% in liver, however they are nearly undetectable in either of these tissues or in the spleens or livers of HDAC7-ΔP mice (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, for full gating see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a profound deficiency in iNKT development.
evidence: This is quantified from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: iNKT cells are nearly undetectable in thymus, spleen, or liver of HDAC7-ΔP mice.
source: Cells positive for staining with CD1D/αGalCer tetramers represent approximately 3% of TCRβ-positive cells in wild type C57BL/6 (B6) thymus and 30% in liver, however they are nearly undetectable in either of these tissues or in the spleens or livers of HDAC7-ΔP mice (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, for full gating see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a profound deficiency in iNKT development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The near absence of iNKT cells in HDAC7-ΔP mice suggests a profound deficiency in iNKT development.
source: Cells positive for staining with CD1D/αGalCer tetramers represent approximately 3% of TCRβ-positive cells in wild type C57BL/6 (B6) thymus and 30% in liver, however they are nearly undetectable in either of these tissues or in the spleens or livers of HDAC7-ΔP mice (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, for full gating see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a profound deficiency in iNKT development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the flow cytometry data showing near-complete absence of iNKT cells.

claim: There are consistently more cells detected in the thymus of HDAC7-ΔP transgenic mice with αGalCer-loaded tetramer than with empty tetramer.
source: There were however consistently more cells detected in the thymus of HDAC7-ΔP transgenic mice with αGalCer-loaded tetramer than with empty tetramer (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D), suggesting that iNKT cells are not entirely absent in this background.
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: iNKT cells are not entirely absent in HDAC7-ΔP mice.
source: There were however consistently more cells detected in the thymus of HDAC7-ΔP transgenic mice with αGalCer-loaded tetramer than with empty tetramer (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D), suggesting that iNKT cells are not entirely absent in this background.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between loaded and empty tetramer staining.

claim: The few thymic tetramer-reactive cells from HDAC7-ΔP mice are evenly distributed between CD44hi/NK1.1+, CD44hi/NK1.1-, and CD44lo/NK1.1- populations.
source: Analyzing these cells according to the conventional staging system for iNKT development (Stritesky et al., 2012), we found that rather than being predominantly CD44hi/NK1.1+ (Stage 3), as in the case of WT iNKT cells, the few thymic tetramer-reactive cells from HDAC7-ΔP mice were evenly distributed between the CD44hi/NK1.1+, CD44hi/NK1.1- (Stage 2), and CD44lo/NK1.1- (Stage 0–1) populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: WT iNKT cells are predominantly CD44hi/NK1.1+ (Stage 3).
source: Analyzing these cells according to the conventional staging system for iNKT development (Stritesky et al., 2012), we found that rather than being predominantly CD44hi/NK1.1+ (Stage 3), as in the case of WT iNKT cells, the few thymic tetramer-reactive cells from HDAC7-ΔP mice were evenly distributed between the CD44hi/NK1.1+, CD44hi/NK1.1- (Stage 2), and CD44lo/NK1.1- (Stage 0–1) populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data comparing WT and HDAC7-ΔP iNKT cells.

claim: The Stage 0-1 population in HDAC7-ΔP mice is predominantly CD24hi.
source: Further analysis of the Stage 0–1 population showed these cells to be predominantly CD24hi, indicating a profound reduction in numbers at all developmental stages that were detectable above background (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a profound reduction in iNKT cell numbers at all developmental stages detectable above background in HDAC7-ΔP mice.
source: Further analysis of the Stage 0–1 population showed these cells to be predominantly CD24hi, indicating a profound reduction in numbers at all developmental stages that were detectable above background (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the CD24 expression pattern and overall low numbers of iNKT cells.

claim: All iNKT populations other than CD24hi/CD44lo/NK1.1- cells are highly underrepresented in HDAC7-ΔP mice after enrichment.
source: Examining these stages after ~20 fold enrichment of iNKT cells using tetramer and magnetic beads, we noted the same pattern, with all populations other than CD24 hi /CD44lo/NK1.1- cells being highly underrepresented (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The iNKT phenotype in HDAC7-ΔP mice is consistent with either a developmental block before Stage one or a severe defect in survival or normal proliferation of iNKT cells from Stage one onwards.
source: These results are consistent with either a developmental block before Stage one or a severe defect in the survival or normal proliferation of iNKT cells from Stage one onwards.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the staging data showing accumulation at early stages.

claim: There is a marked reduction in CD44/NK1.1-expressing T cells that are not tetramer-reactive in liver and spleen of HDAC7-ΔP mice.
source: We also evaluated the prevalence of CD44/NK1.1-expressing T cells that were not tetramer-reactive, and noted a marked reduction in their numbers in liver and spleen as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F), suggesting a broad defect in the development of the NKT lineage.
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: The reduction in non-tetramer-reactive CD44/NK1.1-expressing T cells suggests a broad defect in the development of the NKT lineage in HDAC7-ΔP mice.
source: We also evaluated the prevalence of CD44/NK1.1-expressing T cells that were not tetramer-reactive, and noted a marked reduction in their numbers in liver and spleen as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F), suggesting a broad defect in the development of the NKT lineage.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of reduced type II NKT cells.

claim: The HDAC7-ΔP transgenic population contributes robustly to the pool of CD4 and CD8 SP thymocytes in mixed bone marrow chimeras.
source: As we previously reported (Kasler et al., 2012), the HDAC7-ΔP transgenic population contributed robustly to the pool of CD4 and CD8 SP thymocytes, although there was a transient reduction in prevalence at the immature single positive (ISP) stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in data from mixed chimeras in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is a transient reduction in prevalence of HDAC7-ΔP cells at the immature single positive (ISP) stage in mixed bone marrow chimeras.
source: As we previously reported (Kasler et al., 2012), the HDAC7-ΔP transgenic population contributed robustly to the pool of CD4 and CD8 SP thymocytes, although there was a transient reduction in prevalence at the immature single positive (ISP) stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: At early time points post-reconstitution (6-8wk), the distributions of naïve and memory T-cells in peripheral CD4+ and CD8+ Tconv subsets are equivalent between WT and HDAC7-ΔP populations in mixed chimeras.
source: At early time points post-reconstitution (6-8wk), the distributions of naïve and memory T-cells in peripheral CD4 +and CD8+Tconv subsets were equivalent as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Wild type-derived bone marrow reconstitutes hepatic iNKT cells efficiently in mixed chimeras.
source: However, while the wild type-derived population reconstituted hepatic iNKT cells efficiently, HDAC7-ΔP bone marrow made almost no contribution to this compartment in the liver, where iNKT cells are most abundant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data from mixed chimeras in Figure 1E.

claim: HDAC7-ΔP bone marrow makes almost no contribution to the hepatic iNKT compartment in mixed chimeras.
source: However, while the wild type-derived population reconstituted hepatic iNKT cells efficiently, HDAC7-ΔP bone marrow made almost no contribution to this compartment in the liver, where iNKT cells are most abundant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data from mixed chimeras in Figure 1E.

claim: HDAC7-ΔP bone marrow makes almost no contribution to thymic and splenic iNKT compartments in mixed chimeras.
source: This was also true in the thymus and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), demonstrating that the abnormalities observed in the intact transgenic mice were due to a cell-autonomous mechanism.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The iNKT abnormalities observed in intact HDAC7-ΔP transgenic mice are due to a cell-autonomous mechanism.
source: This was also true in the thymus and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), demonstrating that the abnormalities observed in the intact transgenic mice were due to a cell-autonomous mechanism.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mixed chimera experiments showing the defect persists when HDAC7-ΔP cells develop in a WT environment.

claim: Loss of HDAC7 during T cell development increases apoptosis of DP thymocytes leading to inefficient positive selection.
source: We previously reported that loss of HDAC7 during T cell development increased apoptosis of DP thymocytes leading to inefficient positive selection.
evidence: This is based on previously published work (Kasler et al., 2011).

claim: Shortened thymocyte lifespan in Hdac7-KO mice results in a truncation of the TCR Jα repertoire, with distal rearrangements underrepresented.
source: This shortened thymocyte lifespan resulted in a truncation of the TCR Jα repertoire, with distal rearrangements underrepresented (Kasler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on previously published work (Kasler et al., 2011).

claim: Hdac7-KO mice with an endogenous TCR repertoire have 2-5 fold fewer iNKT cells in thymus than WT littermates.
source: It was thus not surprising to find that Hdac7-KO mice with an endogenous TCR repertoire had fewer iNKT cells than WT controls; for example, Hdac7-KO thymus had a 2–5 fold lower abundance of iNKT cells than WT littermates (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 2A.

claim: The reduction in iNKT cells in Hdac7-KO mice is consistent with the degree of underrepresentation of the relatively distal Jα18 TCR segment.
source: This reduction, consistent with the degree of underrepresentation of the relatively distal Jα18 TCR segment we previously noted (Kasler et al., 2011), was similarly observed in the spleen and liver (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the TCR repertoire truncation to the iNKT reduction.

claim: iNKT cells in Hdac7-KO mice have normal expression of CD44 and NK1.1 when staged after magnetic enrichment.
source: Importantly, unlike the residual tetramer-reactive cells in HDAC7-ΔP mice, when staged after magnetic enrichment, iNKT calls in Hdac7-KO mice had normal expression of CD44 and NK1.1, suggesting that their development was not functionally altered. (Fig, 2A, at right).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 2A.

claim: The normal CD44/NK1.1 expression in Hdac7-KO iNKT cells suggests their development is not functionally altered.
source: Importantly, unlike the residual tetramer-reactive cells in HDAC7-ΔP mice, when staged after magnetic enrichment, iNKT calls in Hdac7-KO mice had normal expression of CD44 and NK1.1, suggesting that their development was not functionally altered. (Fig, 2A, at right).
evidence: This is an inference from the normal marker expression pattern.

claim: There is a substantial expansion of a CD44hi Eomes+ population in the mature CD8 SP compartment in the thymus of Hdac7-KO mice.
source: We noted a substantial expansion of a CD44hi Eomes +population in the mature CD8 SP compartment in the thymus (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Peripheral CD8 T cells in Hdac7-KO mice show a substantial increase in CD44 expression.
source: Examination of the peripheral CD8 T cells in these animals also showed a substantial increase in CD44 expression, suggesting an expansion of innate effector CD8 cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 2C.

claim: The increased CD44 expression in peripheral CD8 T cells of Hdac7-KO mice suggests an expansion of innate effector CD8 cells.
source: Examination of the peripheral CD8 T cells in these animals also showed a substantial increase in CD44 expression, suggesting an expansion of innate effector CD8 cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference from the CD44 expression pattern.

claim: Eomes+ innate memory CD8+ cells are typically generated in trans, in response to IL4 secretion by thymic-resident iNKT cells.
source: These cells resemble Eomes +innate memory CD8 +cells that are typically generated in trans, in response to IL4 secretion by thymic-resident iNKT cells (Lee et al., 2013; Weinreich et al., 2010), however as previously noted iNKTcells are depleted rather than expanded in Hdac7-KO mice, and we did not observe a consistent increase in the proportion of PLZF- or Vγ6.3-positive γδ T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C), suggesting a different mechanism.
evidence: This is based on cited literature (Lee et al., 2013; Weinreich et al., 2010).

claim: iNKT cells are depleted rather than expanded in Hdac7-KO mice.
source: These cells resemble Eomes +innate memory CD8 +cells that are typically generated in trans, in response to IL4 secretion by thymic-resident iNKT cells (Lee et al., 2013; Weinreich et al., 2010), however as previously noted iNKTcells are depleted rather than expanded in Hdac7-KO mice, and we did not observe a consistent increase in the proportion of PLZF- or Vγ6.3-positive γδ T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C), suggesting a different mechanism.
evidence: This is shown in earlier data (Figure 2A).

claim: There is no consistent increase in the proportion of PLZF- or Vγ6.3-positive γδ T cells in Hdac7-KO mice.
source: These cells resemble Eomes +innate memory CD8 +cells that are typically generated in trans, in response to IL4 secretion by thymic-resident iNKT cells (Lee et al., 2013; Weinreich et al., 2010), however as previously noted iNKTcells are depleted rather than expanded in Hdac7-KO mice, and we did not observe a consistent increase in the proportion of PLZF- or Vγ6.3-positive γδ T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C), suggesting a different mechanism.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: The expansion of innate effector CD8 cells in Hdac7-KO mice occurs through a different mechanism than trans-generation by iNKT cells.
source: These cells resemble Eomes +innate memory CD8 +cells that are typically generated in trans, in response to IL4 secretion by thymic-resident iNKT cells (Lee et al., 2013; Weinreich et al., 2010), however as previously noted iNKTcells are depleted rather than expanded in Hdac7-KO mice, and we did not observe a consistent increase in the proportion of PLZF- or Vγ6.3-positive γδ T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C), suggesting a different mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of iNKT expansion and lack of other IL4-producing cells.

claim: In 1:1 mixed chimeras, Hdac7-KO thymocytes compete equally through the ISP stage.
source: In 1:1 chimeras, Hdac7-KO thymocytes competed equally through the ISP stage, but thereafter competed poorly and became steadily less abundant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: After the ISP stage, Hdac7-KO thymocytes compete poorly and become steadily less abundant in 1:1 mixed chimeras.
source: In 1:1 chimeras, Hdac7-KO thymocytes competed equally through the ISP stage, but thereafter competed poorly and became steadily less abundant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: There is substantial underrepresentation of Hdac7-KO CD4 SP and mature CD8 SP thymocytes in 1:1 mixed chimeras.
source: This substantial underrepresentation of Hdac7-KO CD4 SP and mature CD8 SP thymocytes in 1:1 chimeras (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B) made analysis at this stage difficult, however their representation in the periphery was sufficient.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: There is a strong increase in CD44 expression in Hdac7-KO-derived vs. WT-derived CD8 T cells in the spleen of mixed chimeras.
source: In the spleen, we saw a strong increase in CD44 expression in the Hdac7-KO-derived vs. to the WT-derived CD8 T cell population (Figure 2D,E), duplicating what we saw in the intact mice and indicating that the phenotypes we observed are likely cell-autonomous.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The increased CD44 expression in Hdac7-KO CD8 T cells in mixed chimeras duplicates what was observed in intact mice.
source: In the spleen, we saw a strong increase in CD44 expression in the Hdac7-KO-derived vs. to the WT-derived CD8 T cell population (Figure 2D,E), duplicating what we saw in the intact mice and indicating that the phenotypes we observed are likely cell-autonomous.
evidence: This is a comparison between intact mouse data (Figure 2C) and chimera data (Figure 2D,E).

claim: The phenotypes observed in Hdac7-KO mice are likely cell-autonomous.
source: In the spleen, we saw a strong increase in CD44 expression in the Hdac7-KO-derived vs. to the WT-derived CD8 T cell population (Figure 2D,E), duplicating what we saw in the intact mice and indicating that the phenotypes we observed are likely cell-autonomous.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of the phenotype in mixed chimeras where Hdac7-KO cells develop alongside WT cells.

claim: Hdac7-KO-derived CD8+ T cells produce much more IFNγ than WT-derived CD8+ T cells after brief ex vivo stimulation in mixed chimeras.
source: To further characterize the phenotype of these cells, we briefly stimulated splenocytes from these chimeras ex vivo, and found that Hdac7-KO-derived CD8 +T cells produced much more IFNγ than WT-derived CD8 +T cells in the same culture, assessed both as percent cytokine-positive (Figure 3F,G) and by median fluorescence intensity (MFI) of cytokine staining (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F,G,H (note: text references Figure 3F,G,H but should be Figure 2F,G,H based on figure order).

claim: CD8+ T cells from Hdac7-KO population have increased expression of CXCR3.
source: CD8 +T cells from Hdac7-KO population also had increased expression of the Eomes-associated chemokine receptor CXCR3 and the trafficking receptor Ly6C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CD8+ T cells from Hdac7-KO population have increased expression of Ly6C.
source: CD8 +T cells from Hdac7-KO population also had increased expression of the Eomes-associated chemokine receptor CXCR3 and the trafficking receptor Ly6C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of HDAC7 results in the aberrant adoption of innate effector programming by CD8 SP thymocytes that would otherwise have exited the thymus as naive Tconv.
source: Loss of HDAC7 thus appears to result in the aberrant adoption of innate effector programming by CD8 SP thymocytes that would otherwise have exited the thymus as naive Tconv.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing increased innate effector markers in Hdac7-KO CD8 cells.

claim: There is a 20-30% increase in the frequency of memory and IL4-secreting cells in the CD4 compartment of Hdac7-KO mice.
source: We observed a much more modest degree of abnormality in the CD4 compartment, comprising a 20–30% increase in the frequency of memory and IL4-secreting cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C), which we hypothesize is due to the greater similarity that CD8 thymic selection bears to NKT selection, in terms of both the similarity of CD1D to Class I MHC and the availability of selecting ligands on all thymocytes rather than just on specialized thymic APC.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: The greater abnormality in CD8 vs CD4 compartment in Hdac7-KO mice is hypothesized to be due to the greater similarity that CD8 thymic selection bears to NKT selection.
source: We observed a much more modest degree of abnormality in the CD4 compartment, comprising a 20–30% increase in the frequency of memory and IL4-secreting cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C), which we hypothesize is due to the greater similarity that CD8 thymic selection bears to NKT selection, in terms of both the similarity of CD1D to Class I MHC and the availability of selecting ligands on all thymocytes rather than just on specialized thymic APC.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the differential effects in CD4 vs CD8 compartments.

claim: Loss of HDAC7 may allow some DP thymocytes to aberrantly adopt the innate effector lineage through some partial analogue of NKT selection.
source: Loss of HDAC7 may thus allow some DP thymocytes to aberrantly adopt this lineage through some partial analogue of NKT selection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: HDAC7 functions as a gatekeeper of innate effector programming.
source: Collectively, our findings with both the Hdac7-KO and HDAC7-ΔP transgenic strains suggest that HDAC7 may function as a gatekeeper of innate effector programming, blocking the functional maturation of iNKT cells when constitutively expressed in the nucleus, and conversely allowing the aberrant acquisition of innate effector characteristics in Conventional T cells when it is conditionally deleted.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from both gain- and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: HDAC7 blocks the functional maturation of iNKT cells when constitutively expressed in the nucleus.
source: Collectively, our findings with both the Hdac7-KO and HDAC7-ΔP transgenic strains suggest that HDAC7 may function as a gatekeeper of innate effector programming, blocking the functional maturation of iNKT cells when constitutively expressed in the nucleus, and conversely allowing the aberrant acquisition of innate effector characteristics in Conventional T cells when it is conditionally deleted.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the HDAC7-ΔP gain-of-function data.

claim: Loss of HDAC7 allows the aberrant acquisition of innate effector characteristics in Conventional T cells.
source: Collectively, our findings with both the Hdac7-KO and HDAC7-ΔP transgenic strains suggest that HDAC7 may function as a gatekeeper of innate effector programming, blocking the functional maturation of iNKT cells when constitutively expressed in the nucleus, and conversely allowing the aberrant acquisition of innate effector characteristics in Conventional T cells when it is conditionally deleted.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Hdac7-KO loss-of-function data.

claim: Expressing the Vα14-Jα18 TCRα transgene greatly increases the frequency of CD1D/αGalCer-reactive thymocytes.
source: Expressing this TCR transgene greatly increases the frequency of CD1D/αGalCer-reactive thymocytes, which arise naturally only at only around 1 in 104 cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the Vα14 transgene and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CD1D/αGalCer-reactive thymocytes arise naturally at only around 1 in 10^4 cells.
source: Expressing this TCR transgene greatly increases the frequency of CD1D/αGalCer-reactive thymocytes, which arise naturally only at only around 1 in 104 cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about iNKT cell frequency.

claim: Mice expressing only the Vα14 transgene have many more iNKT cells in thymus and spleen than WT mice.
source: As expected, mice expressing only the Vα14 transgene had many more iNKT cells in thymus and spleen than WT mice (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Crossing the Vα14 TCRα transgene into the Hdac7-KO strain results in complete rescue of iNKT cell abundance in the thymus and periphery.
source: Also consistent with our expectations, when we crossed the Vα14 TCRα transgene into the Hdac7-KO strain, we observed a complete rescue of iNKT cell abundance in the thymus and periphery (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B), resulting in identical numbers between Vα14 and Vα14 Hdac7-KO mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Vα14 and Vα14 Hdac7-KO mice have identical iNKT cell numbers.
source: Also consistent with our expectations, when we crossed the Vα14 TCRα transgene into the Hdac7-KO strain, we observed a complete rescue of iNKT cell abundance in the thymus and periphery (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B), resulting in identical numbers between Vα14 and Vα14 Hdac7-KO mice.
